item.title: How Polyphenols Help the Gut-Brain Axis
item.description:
Gut-Brain Axis

How Polyphenols Help the Gut-Brain Axis

Plant compounds work with your gut to lower brain inflammation.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Plant compounds called polyphenols found in tea and wine act like prebiotics, food for gut microbes.
  • In the colon, polyphenols produce substances that help heal the gut lining and lower inflammation.
  • Lowering inflammation can keep the brain from creating amyloid plaques that lead to dementia.

“It's been proven by quite a few studies that plants are good for our psychological development. If you green an area, the rate of crime goes down… So we need them, in some deep psychological sense, which I don't suppose anybody really understands yet.” —Jane Goodall

Plants and animals have a complex relationship. Animals eat plants, so wily plants use chemical weapons to fight back.

A hemlock tea killed Socrates, a punishment for asking too many questions. The Roman Emperor Claudius was murdered by poisonous mushrooms served up by his wife, who preferred her son Nero on the throne. Bulgarian dissident Georgi Markov was assassinated by a jab in the leg with ricin, extracted by the KGB from castor beans.

Historically, plants have done a pretty good job of killing people.

But animals also help pollinate flowers and spread seeds around; so some flirting also takes place. Birds and bees are beguiled by nectar, in exchange for pollination services. Sometimes we use a plant’s chemical arsenal to our own advantage. That’s because we have common enemies, like pathogenic microbes. Take polyphenols, for example: plant compounds found in foods like tea, fruit, cocoa, and red wine. They can benefit our immune system and even soothe the brain.

What are polyphenols?

Polyphenols include substances like EGCG, found mainly in green tea, that help ward off dementia. Another polyphenol is resveratrol, found in grapes and berries, that aids in neurological repair. These two polyphenols, EGCG and resveratrol, are gaining attention as plant compounds that may help us age better and smarter.

Source: Jovanmandic / iStock

As we get older, our immune system changes, and not for the better. A creeping inflammation starts to insinuate itself throughout our increasingly leaky body. It is called inflammaging, and it can affect our brain, leading to amyloid plaque buildup, the first step toward dementia.

There are few things in life as dreadful as the inexorable loss of personality that accompanies dementia. Because it leaves people helpless without killing them, it puts an enormous burden on friends and family to care for them.

Our brain has a distinct set of immune cells called microglia. But they lack subtlety and often cause collateral damage as they cruise for pathogens to kill. Damage to nerve cells affects memory and cognition, often permanently. We might destroy all the pathogens yet still lose our minds to over-eager microglia.

Microglia also have a healing mode, though, and some of the damage can be repaired. The beauty of polyphenols is that they can encourage the microglia to spend less time fighting and more time fixing.

Where is the gut connection?

Polyphenols can’t work without the trillions of microbes in your gut called the microbiome. Polyphenols are prebiotics: substances that our bodies can’t digest, but our microbes crave. They make it intact to the colon, where the bulk of the microbiome is housed. There they are broken down into smaller phenolic acids that are anti-inflammatory.

Polyphenols increase the growth of beneficial bacteria like Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus while suppressing pathogens like Clostridium perfringens. Amazingly, some boosted microbes produce neurotransmitters like dopamine, serotonin, and GABA. These molecules are the target of antidepressants, and the fact that tiny microbes make neurotransmitters is a big clue about why we keep them around: They make us feel better.

These beneficial bacteria also produce a remarkable substance called butyrate that acts like chicken soup, both feeding and healing the gut lining. Butyrate also makes it to the brain, where it encourages the growth of new nerve cells and quells inflammation.

The standard American diet (SAD) is largely devoid of prebiotics, starving those useful microbes and leading to gut lining breakdown. This allows toxins and bacteria to enter the bloodstream, pumped dutifully by the heart to every organ in the body, including the brain.

Today, these SAD processed foods account for some 60 percent of our dietary intake, leading to the extinction of beneficial microbes and contributing to the epidemic of depression currently sweeping the globe.

Resveratrol comes to the rescue by boosting populations of good microbes and plugging a leaky gut.

When inflammation is triggered in the body, a master switch flips on, redirecting energy to the immune system. Resveratrol turns the switch back off, lowering inflammation and — via the gut-brain axis — relieving the sickness behavior that makes you want to crawl into bed and pull the covers up.

With the help of gut microbes, resveratrol helps to patch up the gut lining, lower inflammation, and initiate brain repair.

The brain in its ivory tower

Our pampered and privileged brain is separated from our coarse body by the blood-brain barrier (BBB) to keep the riffraff out. But under prolonged assault by microbes — as well as the immune cells fighting them — the BBB can break down, allowing toxins and microbes to enter the brain. Then all hell breaks loose, and microglia suit up for war. That’s where EGCG comes in, toning down the typical commando response into more nuanced policing action. It also acts as a mediator, pushing the microglia into repair mode.

Most of what we know about polyphenols comes from rodent studies. What about people?

The human angle

For humans, the evidence is trickling in, and it is generally positive. A recent meta-analysis of 13 trials found that polyphenol supplements, including EGCG and resveratrol, consistently improved cognition. Resveratrol also showed encouraging results with Alzheimer’s. Importantly, the Mediterranean diet, high in polyphenols, is associated with slower cognitive decline.

But the underlying studies were all over the map, with incompatible dosing and testing. We need consistent studies to bring this into regular practice. There are some caveats. High doses of EGCG have been linked to liver injury, especially when taken on an empty stomach. Resveratrol, on the other hand, has a good safety record and has been given to patients with Alzheimer disease at up to 1 gram twice daily.

Talk to your doctor before you start using polyphenol supplements, especially if you are already taking psychoactive drugs or have active flare-ups of IBS or IBD.

Our relationship with plants may be fraught, but it can also be fruitful, especially with the help of a healthy microbiome. The right plants with the right microbes may be the key to a long, healthy life.

item.title: Your To-Do List Might Be the Problem
item.description:
Executive Function

Your To-Do List Might Be the Problem

How changing your to-do list system, even shortening your list, can help.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • A good to-do list captures tasks, schedules them, and reminds you to do them.
  • To-do lists can become overwhelming when they are disorganized or overwhelming.
  • You can prioritize your tasks by urgency or impact on your life.

We’re watching our go-to feel-good show, Bob’s Burgers, when the parents make an incredibly relatable joke. Instead of cleaning up after a big, messy party, they suggest moving apartments. The task is so overwhelming that avoiding it altogether seems like the only logical solution.

Until recently, my to-do list was like that. A massive, multi-page mash-up of home, work, social life, health, and other adulting tasks in three unlabeled columns. When out of space, I put items in the margins or sideways, making the visual even more overwhelming. Logically, I tried to never look at it. Yet, the pages’ mere existence stoked a flame of worry and stress, nagging me constantly to get the tasks done.

Now might be a good time to remind you that I’m an executive function coach. I literally help people learn to organize, plan, prioritize, and yes, use lists. Yet my personal system had morphed into a mess that was undermining, not serving me. I needed to make a change.

A to-do list can empower a smart schedule
Source: Pexels by freestocks.org

As I took a leap of faith and looked at my to-do list pages, I realized that they were miscategorized. They were my holding tank, my idea and obligation list, but they were not my to-do list. The functional to-dos were on my calendar, scheduled for the day so I would make time for and remember what I needed to do. Calling the large list “to-do” created a mental expectation that made me avoid using it as the tool it was: my brain on paper, a place from which I could pull my actual tasks. You may also be accidentally making your to-do list your enemy.

Refresh your to-do list system

First, consider that your full task system usually represents three components: capture, schedule, and remind. A great to-do system captures the necessary tasks, puts them in your schedule with reasonable time estimates, and reminds you of the schedule and commitments. Does it serve its purpose if it doesn't include specific times? You can time-block your tasks and set reminders or alarms for the major ones.

Reflect on how realistic your list is. You could technically write “fly to the moon” on your to-do list, but unless you’re an astronaut with a scheduled trip, it won’t be realistic. The same goes for more common earthly examples. We may add, “Go to Costco” during a 15-minute work break, but we all know how realistic that is. We often overload our list with too many tasks or don’t account for the set-up and transition times for each one. Paradoxically, being realistic about what you can accomplish in one day sets you up for more efficiency; you don’t lose time to frustrations or force yourself to reschedule when you realize the unrealistic demands you put on yourself.

Lastly, consider how your list reflects your priorities. When I’m planning my days, I often start with items in the main task list by order of urgency. Is someone waiting for a reply, or is there a hard deadline? Would getting the task done be a huge, immediate relief? There’s a flipside to that, too. I ask myself if I’m drawn to a non-urgent task because it will help me engage in productive procrastination; doing busy work to avoid the real, necessary work. Other ways to prioritize tasks as you plan include considering the tasks’ impact on your finances, relationships, well-being, and values. And while that sounds like a moral assessment, each of us is in a different chapter of life, with varying priorities. There’s no wrong way to prioritize tasks, so long as you’re checking in with your values and goals.

To-do lists anchor us, and strong systems help us capture our tasks, schedule them, and remind our future selves to do them. Updating your system refreshes your approach, making you feel in control and less overwhelmed.

item.title: Floods of Water and Information, Which Is More of a Risk?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Floods of Water and Information, Which Is More of a Risk?

Thinking about climate change and artificial intelligence.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Climate change and artificial intelligence both pose threats, but we evaluate their risks differently.
  • Risk assessments are influenced by how uncontrollable, catastrophic, widespread, and unfair a threat appears.
  • We need to be logical about the risks they pose and willing to view both as a problem to be solved.

If I were to ask you which you fear most, climate change or artificial intelligence (AI), you might have to think for a bit about your response. In part, your answer would depend on how much you know about each topic, and how much you think each phenomenon might pose a threat to you or people you care about. So how do public perceptions of these two differing threats compare?

The first, climate change isn’t a new concern. Throughout human history, the world has undergone major shifts in the weather. Human records, geological research, and data such as the growth rings in redwood trees suggest that floods, droughts, and extreme weather events have long been a concern. But a growing body of research indicates that during the 21st century, global air and water temperatures have been rising and our weather patterns have been changing at unprecedented rates. Extreme heat, unusual rain levels, melting ice, and unpredictable storms are changing our coastlines, destroying our homes and the lives of both humans and animals.

While it is difficult to deny this evidence, we continue to debate whether the changes are natural or manmade, fueling debates about the reliability of the science, the ability of governments to respond and the economic costs both of ignoring and trying to mitigate warming temperatures. Nevertheless, according to the 2026 Yale Climate survey, 68 percent of Americans now believe that climate change is occurring, and 47 percent believe it is harming the United States now. The results of a recent YouGov poll indicate that about 25 percent of Americans think climate change will ultimately cause the extinction of the human race.

In contrast to climate change, artificial intelligence is a new and emerging threat. The field itself was officially established as an academic discipline in 1956, but it took the advent of the internet, personal computers, cell phones and interactive technology to bring it into the average person’s life. We have all derived at least some benefit from rapid access to information and communication via the news media, academic sources, and social media sites. But it was one thing to think of “intelligent computers” trolling through information to collect and combine it for us, and another to think that machines could use that information to create original content.

Of course, the reality is that the answers they produce are only as good as the information they have accessed. The ways their search engines are configured, the biases of the people or machines that produced their source data, and the way they organize materials can all impact the final product. Another problem is their tendency to include incomplete, incorrect, or even blatantly false information, sometimes referred to as hallucinations, into their final results.

These issues are routinely being discussed in the news, as part of corporate, political, and educational discussions, and a number of individuals involved in the development of AI have spoken openly about the concerns they have about its use. In a Pew Poll, 51 percent of Americans reported that they are more concerned than excited about AI. In a September Poll by Politico, 63 percent of Americans said that there was either a moderate, significant, or certain risk that AI would cause human extinction.

From a psychological point of view, it is interesting to consider why at least half of Americans are concerned about both issues but are more likely to see AI as an existential threat to humanity than climate change. Fortunately, the work of psychologist Paul Slovic sheds some interesting light on this finding. Slovic’s decades of research on risk perception indicate that people don’t simply evaluate risk in terms of numerical probabilities. Instead, they assess factors such as how controllable the perceived threat is, how familiar they are with the source of the risk, how fatal and widespread its effects are likely to be, and who it is going to affect.

So how do climate change and AI compare on these criteria? Humans tend to view natural and manmade disasters in different ways. We actually use the phrase “act of God” to describe weather events and will concede that there are some things we just can’t change. When we believe something was caused by people, we assume that it could have gone differently and feel even more distressed. In addition, we are all more familiar with the weather than with artificial intelligence and are accustomed to thinking of it as a localized phenomenon, not a global one. AI is novel to most of us, and we don’t really understand how it works or what its implications are, making it difficult to figure out how to prevent problems. As a result, many of us feel more uneasy about AI than climate change, even though they both pose significant risks to our future well-being.

Although public perception doesn’t predict how much impact a risk will eventually have on a society, it does influence how much time, energy, and money we put into mitigating the problem. Although climate change seems more familiar, and we can tell ourselves it is an act of nature, our behaviors can impact how damaging it becomes. Similarly, artificial intelligence is still evolving, and we need to be mindful of its impacts. Fortunately, humans are resilient and adaptable. We have weathered the industrial revolution and continue to seek ways to manage the threat of nuclear war. But it is becoming increasingly clear that we need to take both climate change and artificial intelligence just as seriously.

This is not to say we need to panic or lose all hope for the future. Instead, we need to approach both as issues that require open discussion, informed problem-solving, and resource allocation. Climate change and artificial intelligence are not the stuff of science-fiction novels. They are real-world issues that can be managed. But to do so, we have to be willing to assess our automatic reactions and to develop accurate perceptions of the risks they pose.

item.title: Evaluating the Mass Hysteria Theory of Havana Syndrome
item.description:
Fantasies

Evaluating the Mass Hysteria Theory of Havana Syndrome

Examining the strengths and limits of the mass psychogenic illness argument.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Some experts assert that Havana Syndrome is a classic case of mass psychogenic illness (MPI) not real injury.
  • There is some overlap of symptoms with MPI (e.g. headache) and social contagion may be a viable vector.
  • However, MPI does not explain much of the data from studies of victims, and remains an unproven hypothesis.

Havana Syndrome, also known as anomalous health incidents (AHIs), represents a cluster of acute and chronic neurological symptoms such as headache, imbalance, vertigo, and cognitive problems. [1]

Two prestigious expert panels, one from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine and another from the Intelligence Community, concluded that pulsed radiofrequency energy could plausibly account for some distinctive AHI symptoms. [2, 3]

However, the expert panels were unable to pinpoint an exact mechanism of injury. Moreover, although some medical studies reported objective differences in AHI patients, others did not. [4, 5]

The lack of clarity about the cause of AHI symptoms and the inconsistent results led some experts to assert that AHI represents a case of mass hysteria, formally known as mass psychogenic illness (MPI). [6]

What is Mass Psychogenic Illness (MPI)?

MPI is the rapid spread of physical symptoms through a cohesive social group in the absence of an identifiable organic cause, propagated by visual, verbal, or media transmission of belief and anxiety. [7]

MPI spreads through social networks rather than according to proximity to a source, with a predominance among females and younger people. Typically, the index case is someone with high status or visibility. [7]

Common symptoms include headache, dizziness, nausea, hyperventilation, fainting, chest tightness, weakness, paresthesias, and abdominal pain. Motor forms add tremor, tics, psychogenic seizures, gait disturbance, and dysphonia. [7]

Four examples cited in the literature are:

  • Tanganyika laughter epidemic, 1962 — uncontrollable laughing and crying spread through mission schools for months, forcing closures. [8]
  • West Bank schoolgirls, 1983 — nearly 1,000 Palestinians, mostly girls, reported fainting, headache, and abdominal pain; competing allegations of poison gas circulated, but investigators found no toxic cause. [9]
  • Le Roy, NY, 2011–12 — Tourette-like tics emerged among high-school girls; environmental hypotheses were investigated, and social media may have contributed to the spread. [10]
  • Contemporary “TikTok tics” (2020–21) — functional tic-like behaviors were reported in young people during a period of extensive social-media exposure, showing that the “group” need not be physically co-located. [11]

MPI researchers describe underlying psychological mechanisms that include: [7]

  • The nocebo effect (experiencing an adverse result one expects)
  • Heightened attention to interoceptive cues, amplifying ordinary sensations until they seem pathological
  • Acute stress and autonomic arousal, with subsequent reactions interpreted as signs of illness
  • Automatic, unconscious mimicry and “social contagion”
  • A compelling narrative: “Y caused X.”

The case for MPI causing Anomalous Health Experiences

Medical sociologist Dr. Robert Bartholomew and neurologist Dr. Robert Baloh argue in their book, Havana Syndrome: Mass Psychogenic Illness and the Real Story Behind the Embassy Mystery and Hysteria, that AHI is a classic example of MPI. [6]

Indeed, there is overlap between the symptoms of AHI and those reported in some cases of MPI, such as headache, dizziness, and nausea. There is also overlap with some proposed predisposing conditions for MPI, such as social contagion through the news, acute stress, and a narrative that directed-energy weapons wielded by foreign adversaries caused AHI.

Bartholomew and Baloh discount the possibility that pulsed RF or toxins could be responsible, arguing, for instance, that there is no evidence such an RF weapon is possible. Bartholomew went so far as to call proposed RF attacks “science fiction” and to say that “humans have a remarkable capacity for self-deception.” [6, 12]

Dr. Baloh went further: “The idea that a sonic weapon caused selective brain or inner ear damage is not physically possible…” [13]

The case against Mass Psychogenic Illness

As the former Associate Director of National Intelligence overseeing science and technology for the entire Intelligence Community, and author of The Spy in Moscow Station (which describes Russian microwave attacks on U.S. embassies), I am far less confident than Bartholomew and Baloh that an RF weapon capable of causing AHI is physically impossible.

In fact, I recently published a piece on this site describing how, through proposed mechanisms of brain damage such as cavitation and mechanical deformation of brain parenchyma, a pulsed RF weapon could inflict injury. [14]

Together with my wife, Chris Gilbert, MD, PhD, I have developed and tested a high-fidelity simulation of the head, brain, and inner ear that encompasses pulsed RF field concentration in tissue, heat generation in that tissue, pressure buildup from that heat, thermoacoustic pressure transients, and tissue strain and deformation produced by thermoacoustic pressure waves inside the skull. Our results suggest --but do not prove--multiple plausible mechanisms by which pulsed RF could inflict injury, consistent with reports from AHI patients. Our results echo and extend those of Army Research Laboratory scientists exploring the effects of pulsed RF on the brain. [15]

Representation of RF/Thermal/Acosutic model
Source: Eric Haseltine with Chat GPT

But let’s put that aside for the moment—along with press reports that a U.S. government agency acquired a suspected AHI-related RF device and that the Pentagon tested it—and consider the MPI hypothesis on its merits. [16] There are multiple aspects of the AHI story that do not align with the MPI theory:

  • An NSA employee reported an incident predating the highly publicized Havana cases. Social contagion from reports about Havana cannot explain an earlier report. [17]
  • The sudden onset of acute pain, pressure, ear fullness, and directional sounds reported in AHI cases differs from the symptoms typically described in MPI outbreaks. [1, 2, 7]
  • Multiple AHI patients report that symptoms started when they entered a particular area, stopped when they left, and started again when they reentered. [1, 18]
  • Several medical studies reported objective clinical findings, including vestibular and oculomotor abnormalities, although later studies did not find corresponding group differences on all measures. [18, 19]
  • Autopsy studies of people who experienced brain trauma have identified microscopic damage despite unremarkable gross examination, showing that physical injury can be difficult to detect with routine assessment. [20]
  • Several individuals reported symptom onset while alone, at night, in their own residences, before they knew of a wider group of cases. This raises a question about how social transmission would account for the earliest reports. [2, 18]
  • Classic MPI outbreaks can be explosive and self-limiting, with remission after separation and reassurance. A subset of Havana patients have reported symptoms persisting for years despite dispersal and treatment. [2, 7, 19]
  • MPI often spreads through social networks; early Havana cases involved personnel who reported limited awareness of one another’s symptoms. [2, 7]
  • Some affected individuals report having been dismissive of colleagues’ claims before their own onset—the reverse of the expectation a nocebo explanation would require. [2]

What does it all mean?

The MPI hypothesis represents a valid possibility that cannot be entirely discounted simply because it does not explain multiple AHI phenomena.

Given that more than a thousand government employees have reported AHI symptoms, it is possible that at least some of them may have been experiencing MPI. [21]

But the balance of the evidence—even discounting objective medical findings and the conclusions of expert panels that considered the pulsed RF hypothesis—weighs against MPI as the sole cause of AHI.

Certainly, even though the mechanism of AHI injury remains uncertain, there is enough doubt about the MPI theory that statements calling physical causes of AHI “science fiction” or “impossible” seem to go further than the data warrant.

That is why my wife, Chris, and I, who are deeply involved in AHI research and have interviewed half a dozen people reporting AHI, are careful about the language we use to describe our results. We acknowledge substantial gaps in scientific knowledge about how pulsed RF affects the brain and vestibular system.

We use terms such as “possible,” “plausible,” and occasionally “likely” or “unlikely,” but we avoid absolutes such as “science fiction” or “physically impossible.”

One reason is that, if there is a physical cause of AHI, confident assertions that “it’s all in the victims’ heads” risk doubly victimizing people who have already suffered.

We do not want to add to the suffering of people who report AHI, some of whom have seen their careers end or suffer because they spoke up, in addition to experiencing physical and emotional distress.

It is one thing to suffer; it is quite another to have the reality of your suffering discounted with absolute certainty.

Thus, Chris and I try to live by the old saying: “Keep your words soft and sweet. You never know which ones you’ll eat."

item.title: Are You for AI or Against AI?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Are You for AI or Against AI?

A benchmark for using AI well—whether it brings out the best that is human.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Asking if you're for or against AI captures the ambivalence most of us feel, but doesn't help us use it well.
  • Zhēn (真), a Chinese character for "true nature," offers a benchmark: Does a use of AI bring out our best?
  • Most AI systems default toward agreement, and you can counter-configure them for critical assessment.

You likely use AI and find it in certain ways efficient, helpful, and occasionally seemingly brilliant. I do. Sometimes I feel like it lights up my brain.

You may also find AI enormously frustrating as it flattens your ideas and dulls your thinking, as if it’s stripping away parts of your essential self. And you may be thinking, “Regardless of what I think, AI is happening, and if I don’t keep using it and keeping up with it, I’m going to be left behind in the job market.”

Thus, in my post’s title—Are you for AI or against AI?—I provided the answer that I think many of us would, which is “Yes.” The question captures psychological ambivalence. But it doesn’t go far enough to provide ways to understand the fundamental characteristics and pitfalls of AI. And that’s important, because with those in hand, we can better design and use AI well, by which I mean wisely—to bring out the best that is human in terms of intelligence, authenticity, relationality, creativity, morality, and sparkle.

That is what this blog is about. And I have named it with a word that may be unfamiliar to you.

The Chinese character Zhēn (真) means true, real, or genuine. In Daoist thought, it points toward what is authentic when social conventions and artifice no longer dominate. In Chan Buddhism, it appears in expressions such as “true mind” and “true suchness,” alongside teachings about our original nature and an awareness unobscured by conditioned thinking. Across both traditions, Zhēn evokes what is genuine rather than contrived. In English, perhaps the closest simple rendering is “true nature.”

Zhēn (真): true, real, genuine.
Source: Arlas! it / Wikimedia Commons (public domain), AI-upscaled for resolution

I will use the term in this blog, though I would like to update it for our modern technological world.

As I’ve argued elsewhere (Kahn, 2011), we’re a technological species, and always have been. By technology I mean any human artifact that helps us achieve an effect in the world. The San digging stick is a technology: about three feet long, pointed at one end, and excellent for digging roots in the Kalahari because it is light and you can feel what you are doing in the Earth.

For most of our history, our technologies were rudimentary enough that they didn’t intrude much on the question of who we are. AI does. And so Zhēn, if it is going to name our true nature now, has to make space for our technological selves. That is also what makes it a benchmark for designing and using AI well.

Here is one practice that follows from the Zhēn of AI.

Configure Your AI for Critical Feedback

Most commercial AI systems default toward agreement. When you lean toward a direction in your phrasing, tone, or framing of a question, most AI will generate reasons to support where you’re already going, rather than giving you the strongest critical read of the situation.

In current parlance, AI often flatters the user.

This can be effective in certain situations. If you’re brainstorming at a fast pace with it, for example, you probably want AI (or a person) to be generative, and to have the “collaborative other” naming and supporting the good parts it sees in your work.

But for most of your other work, it’s good to have some hard-nosed assessments.

There are many solutions to this problem, and I’ll speak of others in future posts—such as iterative Socratic-like prompting. But a simple one is this: Counter-configure your AI for critical feedback. A configuration might read: “I need critical assessments of ways forward, not only validation. When I’m drawn to a direction, don’t reach for reasons to support it just because I’m leaning that way. Give me the strongest critical read first, including the case against my instinct when it exists. I may override your judgment and then ask for your help making my chosen position as strong as possible. That’s a separate mode. Default mode is critical assessment, even when it’s a little uncomfortable for me.”

Then save it. Most systems let you store a custom instruction or memory setting, so this becomes the default for your serious work.

Now Test Your New Configuration

Take a piece of writing that you’re working on (or that you wrote recently) and ask AI for feedback twice. First with default settings and a neutral prompt: “What do you think of this?” Second, after adding the configuration described above, use the same prompt. Compare the two responses. Ask yourself: Which feedback was more useful? Which was more comfortable? Which helped me more to figure out ways to improve my ideas, or to deepen my perceptions? And was the most comfortable response also the most useful one?

Even with the configuration in place, you’ll find AI sometimes reverting to validation, and when you recognize it, you can call it out. For example, I have sometimes said versions of this to AI: “Your response just now sounds more like flattery than reality. Give me four counterarguments to my position, rank ordered by what you think is most useful for what I’m trying to do here.”

In a small way, this is the Zhēn of AI. We are configuring the machine, directing it, and sometimes collaborating with it, so that it helps us toward greater clarity of mind, clarity of expression, and truthfulness. That is part of what it means to cultivate our true nature.

Disclosure: The author serves as Founding Research & AI Advisor to Scholar Spark, an education company. This blog is independent of that role and unpaid by the company.

item.title: The Problem With Superintelligence
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The Problem With Superintelligence

Calling AI “super” may turn capability into authority.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • “Superintelligence” assumes human and machine intelligence sit on the same cognitive scale.
  • AI may represent a fundamentally different architecture, where performance does not equal wisdom or authority.
  • Calling AI “super” may reshape our relationship with it, encouraging deference and cognitive surrender.
Source: BrownMantis / Pixabay

President Donald Trump, by executive order, has changed the language used by the federal government from “Artificial Intelligence” to “Superintelligence.” On the surface, this may seem like just a change in terminology. But I believe that the word “super” carries with it an assumption that may be more consequential than just a name change.

A few months ago, I wrote a post titled “We’re Measuring AI on the Wrong Ruler.” My argument was rather simple. When we suggest that AI is smarter than humans, we have already made an assumption that human cognition and machine intelligence can be measured on the same line. In this context, we begin to imagine intelligence itself on a single continuum, a bit like measuring it on a number line or axis.

There’s something historically familiar about the word super, and it’s a good place to start. In the early days of nuclear weapons, the hydrogen bomb was coined “the Super.” This weapon was understood to be vastly more powerful than the atomic bomb. And the term made sense because the explosive yield was measured using the same scale. More energy meant a more powerful bomb. But I’m not sure intelligence works that way. Calling AI “super intelligent” leverages a similar word but hardly measures something as objective as kilotons of TNT.

So, this new language of superintelligence may take this assumption into new territory. “Super” establishes a hierarchy where AI is moving up along the same “line” that measures human intelligence. In this structure, it can occupy a position above us. But I’m uncertain (and uncomfortable) that this is the right way to understand what’s actually happening. Lumping artificial computation with human cognition is, to say the least, an oversimplification of both.

I’ve written about Anti-Intelligence as a term to discuss the possibility that AI represents a fundamentally different cognitive architecture that might force us to reconsider the “single line” perspective. And without getting into the complexities of quadrants and orthogonality, here’s the key point: AI can generate remarkable ideas without having the lived experience of human thought.

I believe this difference becomes more important as AI becomes more powerful. But performance and wisdom are very different things. Being very good at solving problems doesn’t automatically grant AI newfound authority. In fact, it’s essential that we recognize that computational power doesn’t confer moral authority even when AI is placed above human capacity.

Here’s where the language itself becomes interesting. If we begin describing AI as super intelligent, we may begin to change our relationship with it. If AI is positioned “above us” intellectually, deference to it might just follow along. Why struggle with a problem ourselves? Why challenge AI’s answers when it’s “linguistically validated” to be our cognitive superior? The “super” label may even transform “super” capability into a sort of intellectual status like the new Ivy League or the better Nobel Prize. And don’t forget, intellectual status often shares a border with authority (or finds its way there).

To me, the critical issue isn’t simply if “Superintelligence” is a better name for AI. Beyond that, we need to ask what happens to our human cognition when we begin structuring our relationship with “a machine” that has advanced past us on that cognitive number line.

So, maybe we are still using the wrong ruler. And if we place AI at the top of that ruler and call it super intelligent, we need to be very careful about our assumptions on all that rests below—particularly ourselves.
